audit_findings.title: SAP settlement cash may be added before deducting taxes and unpaid fees
audit_findings.magnitude: $121 million of fees recognized and paid; $67 million net discrete tax expense; $22 million of settlement-related cash taxes paid; any remaining cash claim unquantified
audit_findings.mechanism: Unpaid settlement taxes or fees would reduce the $414 million cash added in the equity bridge.
audit_findings.evidence: Teradata believes that the net cash benefit of the Settlement Amount after associated fees and expenses, including a customary contingent fee arrangement and other outstanding legal fees incurred in connection with the Litigation, will be in the range of approximately $355–$362 million before taxes (the "Net Proceeds").
audit_findings.explanation: The latest 10-Q resolves the fee concern: Teradata received $480 million and paid $121 million of related expenses, leaving $359 million before tax. Tax remains unresolved because only $22 million of settlement-related cash taxes had been paid, while the filing recorded $67 million of net discrete tax expense; the record does not identify how much of the difference is an unpaid cash liability versus noncash deferred-tax usage. Therefore, no bridge error is yet demonstrated and its materiality cannot be established.
audit_findings.action: Reconcile the settlement tax provision into cash paid, deferred-tax usage, refunds or credits, and current tax payable at June 30, 2026; deduct any unpaid cash tax attributable to the settlement from the bridge.

audit_findings.title: The share ceiling may not include maximum PSU payouts
audit_findings.mechanism: PSU settlements above the quantities included in the 103.604 million fully diluted denominator would increase shares and reduce value per share.
audit_findings.evidence: In the event the objectives are exceeded, additional shares will vest up to a maximum payout.
audit_findings.explanation: The filing demonstrates that PSU quantities can increase above target, but it does not provide aggregate outstanding maximum-payout shares. Consequently, dilution beyond the denominator is possible but neither its existence nor materiality is established. Retaining stock-compensation expense addresses an operating cost, not an omitted equity claim.
audit_findings.action: Compile outstanding PSUs by grant, target units, maximum payout factor and current performance estimate; rerun every scenario using aggregate maximum incremental shares without netting unused ESPP authorization against PSU dilution.

audit_findings.title: Underfunded employee-benefit obligations are omitted from the equity bridge
audit_findings.magnitude: $118 million at December 31, 2025; 5.4% of the $2.167 billion base equity value and $1.14 per share if deducted dollar-for-dollar
audit_findings.mechanism: The funded-status deficit is a claim ahead of common equity and enters as a bridge deduction unless its settlement cash flows are explicitly included in projected owner earnings.
audit_findings.evidence: We also have postemployment and international pension obligations that may affect future cash flow.
audit_findings.explanation: The filing demonstrates a $56 million pension deficit plus a $62 million postemployment deficit, while the stated bridge contains no benefit-obligation deduction. Annual benefit expense does not by itself settle deficits arising from past service and actuarial losses. A dollar-for-dollar deduction would reduce base value from $20.92 to approximately $19.78 per share, a material bridge adjustment.
audit_findings.action: Obtain the June 30, 2026 funded-status calculation, including current and noncurrent amounts, and either deduct the latest net deficit from the bridge or rerun owner earnings with explicit deficit-funding cash flows, avoiding double counting.

audit_findings.title: Financed customer equipment must be included in maintenance investment
audit_findings.magnitude: $77 million of 2025 finance-lease asset additions, equal to 61.7% of the $124.8 million owner-earnings anchor
audit_findings.mechanism: If depreciation is added back while financed equipment additions or an equivalent maintenance charge are omitted, anchor owner earnings and every projected operating value are overstated.
audit_findings.evidence: The Company's finance leases primarily consist of equipment financed for the purpose of delivering services to our customers.
audit_findings.explanation: The equipment is used to deliver customer services, so some economic reinvestment charge is required. The filing establishes $77 million of additions, but the supplied record does not show whether the $124.8 million anchor deducted those additions, finance-lease principal payments, or another equivalent maintenance amount. The possible omission is large relative to the anchor and therefore reasonably capable of materially changing the valuation.
audit_findings.action: Reproduce the $124.8 million anchor line by line and identify the finance-lease charge. If no equivalent charge is present, rerun all scenarios deducting the appropriate maintenance-equipment investment; if principal payments are already used as the economic charge, do not also deduct asset additions.

audit_findings.title: Noncancelable vendor commitments create downside not visible in the OE growth rates
audit_findings.magnitude: $553 million total purchase obligations, including $301 million due in 2026; any excess or onerous portion unquantified
audit_findings.mechanism: Unused minimum commitments would reduce future owner earnings or require a separate charge, making the assumed growth paths too favorable.
audit_findings.evidence: Purchase obligations are committed purchase orders and other contractual commitments for goods and services and include non-cancelable contractual payments for fixed or minimum amounts to be purchased in relation to service agreements with various vendors for ongoing telecommunications, information technology, hosting and other services.
audit_findings.explanation: The commitments are filed amounts, but gross purchase obligations are not equivalent to a loss because they may support revenue and may already be reflected in ordinary operating costs. No excess-capacity or onerous-contract amount is presently demonstrated. This is therefore a forward-looking utilization risk rather than an established adjustment to current owner earnings or the bridge.
audit_findings.action: Map vendor minimums by year and service category against noncancelable customer revenue, expected utilization and forecast operating expenses; rerun scenarios only for identified excess commitments or onerous-contract charges.

audit_findings.title: The latest-year anchor contains a discrete tax benefit
audit_findings.magnitude: $2 million net discrete benefit, 1.6% of the $124.8 million anchor; approximately $28.1 million or $0.27 per share of base value if fully carried into perpetuity
audit_findings.mechanism: An unnormalized one-time tax benefit raises the owner-earnings anchor and proportionally raises projected operating value.
audit_findings.evidence: The 2025 effective tax rate included a net $2 million of discrete tax benefit, of which $9 million of tax benefit resulted from the reversal of unrecognized tax benefits, a majority of which was due to the settlement of the Company's 2020 federal income tax audit in the first quarter.
audit_findings.explanation: The filing reports a $9 million reserve-reversal benefit largely offset by $7 million of stock-compensation tax expense, producing a $2 million net discrete benefit. Whether the existing anchor already normalized it is unresolved, but even complete omission of the net adjustment would reduce base value only from $20.92 to approximately $20.65 per share and would not change the valuation conclusion relative to the $28.05 market price.
audit_findings.action: Reconcile the anchor tax line to the filed $9 million benefit and $7 million expense; if the net $2 million was retained, rerun the scenarios with a consistently normalized tax charge.
